To: Residents of 48 Alder Street
From: Hana Kobayashi
Subject: Safety inspection on October 13

Dear tenants,

As your landlord, I must have every apartment inspected once a year. This year's inspection will take place on Tuesday, October 13, between 9:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. An inspector will test the smoke detectors, check the window locks, and look at the heating system. Hana Kobayashi

router.subject: Urban studies
router.title: Gardens Above the Street
paragraphs: A green roof is a rooftop that is partly or completely covered with living plants. Beneath the plants lie several layers: soil or a lighter growing material, a drainage layer, and a waterproof sheet that protects the building. Grass-covered roofs are centuries old, but the modern version was developed in Germany in the second half of the twentieth century and has since spread worldwide.

The benefits are considerable. During a storm, the soil and plants hold much of the rain and release it slowly, which reduces the pressure on city drains and lowers the risk of flooded streets. In summer, a planted roof stays far cooler than a dark conventional one, so the rooms below need less air conditioning. Green roofs also offer food and shelter to insects and birds in neighborhoods with little open land.

Nevertheless, green roofs are not suitable everywhere. Wet soil is heavy, and many older buildings would have to be strengthened before they could carry it. A green roof also costs more to install than an ordinary one, and its plants need occasional care. For these reasons, some cities offer tax reductions or direct payments to owners who install them, while others require them on large new buildings. Supporters argue that the long-term savings outweigh the initial expense.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How to choose plants for a rooftop garden
The advantages and limits of planted rooftops
Why flooding has become more common in cities
The history of roof construction in Germany
questions.why: Paragraph 2 sets out the benefits; paragraph 3 begins 'Nevertheless, green roofs are not suitable everywhere' and gives the drawbacks.

questions.q: According to the passage, how do green roofs help during storms?
options: They direct rainwater into the rooms below.
They keep rain from reaching the soil.
They store rain and let it go gradually.
They make the city's drains wider.
questions.why: 'The soil and plants hold much of the rain and release it slowly.'

questions.q: The word "considerable" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: large
uncertain
familiar
recent
questions.why: Considerable means large in amount or importance; the paragraph then lists several major benefits.

questions.q: What can be inferred about older buildings?
options: Most of them already have a drainage layer under the roof.
They stay cooler in summer than buildings with planted roofs.
Their owners are not allowed to receive payments from the city.
Many would need structural work before plants could be added.
questions.why: 'Wet soil is heavy, and many older buildings would have to be strengthened before they could carry it.'

questions.q: Why does the author mention tax reductions and direct payments?
options: To argue that green roofs are too expensive to be practical
To explain why older buildings are being replaced
To show how some cities encourage green roofs
To compare German cities with cities in other countries
questions.why: The sentence begins 'For these reasons' (the weight and the cost) and says the money goes 'to owners who install them'.

upper.subject: Anthropology
upper.title: Did Cooking Make Us Human?
paragraphs: The human brain is an expensive organ. Although it makes up only about two percent of body weight, it consumes roughly a fifth of the energy the body uses at rest. How our ancestors managed to feed such a demanding organ is a long-standing puzzle. One influential answer, proposed by the primatologist Richard Wrangham, is that they learned to cook.

Heat softens food and begins to break it down before it is eaten. As a result, the body obtains more energy from a cooked meal than from the same meal raw and spends less effort chewing and digesting it. Wild chimpanzees spend several hours a day simply chewing. According to Wrangham, cooking freed early humans from this burden, and the surplus energy allowed the brain to expand. He links the change to Homo erectus, a species that appeared nearly two million years ago with smaller teeth and a larger brain than its predecessors.

Skeptics point to a gap in the record. Clear traces of controlled fire, such as hearths, are much younger than the first Homo erectus fossils. Some researchers therefore credit other changes, including eating more meat or pounding food with stone tools, for the early growth of the brain. The debate remains open, yet few doubt that cooking, whenever it began, reshaped the human body.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The ways in which chimpanzees and humans digest raw food
The reasons archaeologists find it hard to date ancient fires
The methods scientists use to measure the brain's energy needs
A proposed link between cooking and brain growth
questions.why: The passage presents Wrangham's answer to how the brain was fed ('they learned to cook'), explains it, and then gives the objections.

questions.q: According to the passage, what is one effect of heating food?
options: It removes most of the energy from the food.
It lowers the effort of chewing and digestion.
It makes meat safer to store for long periods.
It causes teeth to grow smaller within a lifetime.
questions.why: With cooked food the body 'spends less effort chewing and digesting it'.

questions.q: The word "surplus" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: necessary
hidden
extra
limited
questions.why: Surplus energy is energy left over beyond what is needed, that is, extra energy.

questions.q: Why does the author mention wild chimpanzees?
options: To illustrate how much time eating raw food can take
To show that some animals have learned to use fire
To suggest that their brains are as large as early humans'
To explain where Wrangham carried out his research
questions.why: 'Wild chimpanzees spend several hours a day simply chewing'; cooking 'freed early humans from this burden'.

questions.q: What does the passage imply about Wrangham's proposal?
options: Nearly all researchers have now rejected it.
Direct evidence for its timing has not been found.
It was based mainly on the study of stone tools.
It claims that cooking began after the brain had grown.
questions.why: 'Clear traces of controlled fire... are much younger than the first Homo erectus fossils', so nothing yet shows fire at the time the theory requires. The debate 'remains open'.

router.subject: Astronomy
router.script: Raise your hand if you learned in school that there are nine planets. OK, quite a few of you. So what happened to number nine? Well, Pluto didn't change. Our definition did. Pluto was discovered in nineteen thirty, and for decades it was simply the ninth planet. But it was always a strange one. It's tiny, smaller than our own Moon, and its orbit is tilted compared with the others. Then, in the nineteen nineties, astronomers started finding more and more icy objects out beyond Neptune, in a region called the Kuiper Belt. And in two thousand five, they found one, later named Eris, that's about the same size as Pluto. So here was the problem. If Pluto's a planet, then Eris is too, and maybe dozens of others. Where do you stop? So in two thousand six, the International Astronomical Union voted on an official definition. A planet has to orbit the Sun, it has to be big enough for its gravity to pull it into a round shape, and it has to have cleared other objects out of its path. Pluto passes the first two tests. But it shares its neighborhood with all those icy bodies, so it fails the third. That's why it's now called a dwarf planet. Not everybody was happy about that, by the way, and some astronomers still argue the definition should change.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How Pluto was discovered in 1930
Why Pluto was put in a new category
What the Kuiper Belt is made of
How astronomers measure the size of planets
questions.why: The professor asks 'what happened to number nine?' and explains the new definition that made Pluto a dwarf planet.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention Eris?
options: To prove that Pluto is larger than the Moon
To show that Neptune has an unusual orbit
To give an example of an object with a tilted orbit
To explain why a definition became necessary
questions.why: 'If Pluto's a planet, then Eris is too, and maybe dozens of others. Where do you stop?' The vote on a definition followed.

questions.q: According to the professor, which test does Pluto fail?
options: Clearing objects from its path
Traveling in an orbit around the Sun
Being pulled into a round shape
Being larger than Earth's Moon
questions.why: Pluto 'passes the first two tests' but 'shares its neighborhood with all those icy bodies, so it fails the third'. Size compared with the Moon is not one of the tests.

questions.q: What does the professor imply about the decision made in 2006?
options: It will be reversed within a few years.
It was based on a mistake about Pluto's size.
Some astronomers still do not accept it.
It was made without a vote.
questions.why: 'Not everybody was happy about that... and some astronomers still argue the definition should change.'

router.subject: Business history
router.script: Let's start with a number. Before nineteen thirteen, it took workers at Henry Ford's factory more than twelve hours to assemble the chassis of one Model T, that's the frame with the engine and wheels. About a year later, it took an hour and a half. What changed? Not the car. What changed was how the work moved. Before, the car stayed in one place, and teams of workers walked around it, fetching parts. Ford's engineers turned that around. They put the car on a moving line and had it travel past the workers. Each person stood in one spot and did one small job, over and over, maybe tightening the same two bolts all day. The results were dramatic. Because cars were faster to build, they were cheaper to build, and the price of a Model T fell year after year, until ordinary families could afford one. But there was a cost. The work was so dull and so tiring that workers kept quitting, and Ford had to keep hiring and training new ones. His answer, in nineteen fourteen, was the five-dollar day, roughly double the usual pay. It worked. People stayed. And, as it happened, with wages like that, his own workers could now buy the cars they were building.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: A change in how cars were put together
Why the Model T was redesigned in 1914
How Henry Ford chose and trained engineers
Why the earliest cars broke down so often
questions.why: 'What changed was how the work moved': the talk describes the moving line and its results.

questions.q: According to the professor, what was new about Ford's system?
options: Teams of workers walked around each car.
Each worker learned to do every job.
The car moved, and the workers did not.
Parts were made in a separate factory.
questions.why: 'They put the car on a moving line and had it travel past the workers. Each person stood in one spot.' A describes the old system.

questions.q: What problem did the new system create?
options: Cars became too expensive for families.
Engineers refused to change the factory.
The cars took longer to build.
Many workers left their jobs.
questions.why: 'The work was so dull and so tiring that workers kept quitting.'

questions.q: What does the professor imply about the five-dollar day?
options: It was lower than the pay at other factories.
It benefited Ford in more than one way.
It forced Ford to raise the price of his cars.
It was introduced before the moving line.
questions.why: It kept workers ('People stayed'), and 'his own workers could now buy the cars they were building', so it also created customers.

upper.subject: Environmental science
upper.script: I'd like to clear up a misconception before we go any further. When people see photos of a bleached reef, all that ghostly white, they tend to assume they're looking at dead coral. They're not. Not yet, anyway. Here's what's going on. A coral is an animal, and living inside its tissue are microscopic algae. It's a partnership. The coral provides shelter, and the algae, through photosynthesis, supply most of the coral's food. They're also what gives a reef its color. Now, when the water stays unusually warm for several weeks, even by just a degree or two, that partnership breaks down. The algae start producing substances that are toxic to their host, and the coral responds by, well, evicting them. What's left is transparent tissue over a white skeleton. Hence, bleaching. So a bleached coral is alive, but it's essentially starving. If the water cools in time, the algae come back and the coral recovers. If it doesn't, the coral dies. And this is where I struggle to sound optimistic. A reef can bounce back from one bad summer, but that takes a decade or so. What we're seeing now are heat waves arriving every few years, which simply doesn't leave enough time. So when you read that a reef has recovered, I'd encourage you to ask: recovered for how long?

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the talk?
options: To describe the fish that live on coral reefs
To argue that bleached reefs can never recover
To compare algae with other ocean plants
To explain what happens when coral bleaches
questions.why: The professor corrects the idea that bleached coral is dead ('Here's what's going on') and describes the process and its outcome. B is wrong because a reef 'can bounce back from one bad summer'.

questions.q: According to the professor, what do the algae give the coral?
options: A hard white skeleton
Most of its food
Protection from warm water
A place to shelter
questions.why: 'The algae, through photosynthesis, supply most of the coral's food.' Shelter is what the coral gives the algae.

questions.q: Why does the professor say this: "Not yet, anyway"?
options: To signal that the coral may still die
To admit that she is unsure of the facts
To show that the photos are out of date
To suggest that the reef was never alive
questions.why: Bleached coral is alive but 'essentially starving'; if the water does not cool, 'the coral dies'. 'Not yet' points ahead to that risk.

questions.q: What is the professor's attitude toward reports that a reef has recovered?
options: She is confident that they are accurate.
She thinks they exaggerate the damage.
She doubts that the recovery will last.
She finds them too technical for the public.
questions.why: 'This is where I struggle to sound optimistic... I'd encourage you to ask: recovered for how long?'

upper.subject: Linguistics
upper.script: Here's something that ought to puzzle us more than it does. Nobody sits a two-year-old down and explains the past tense. And yet, by four or so, virtually every child is using it. So how do they pull that off? The obvious guess is imitation. Children just copy what they hear. But listen to the mistakes they make. A child will say 'I goed to the park' or 'two foots.' Now, no adult says 'goed.' The child can't be copying. What she's done is work out a rule, put a 'd' sound on the end for the past, and apply it a little too enthusiastically. There's a lovely experiment from the nineteen fifties that makes the same point. The researcher, Jean Berko, showed young children a drawing of an imaginary creature and said, 'This is a wug.' Then she showed them two. 'Now there are two...' And the children said 'wugs.' They'd never heard that word in their lives, so they couldn't have memorized its plural. And interestingly, when parents do correct their children, it tends to be about facts, not grammar. Call a dog a cat, and you'll be corrected. Say something true in broken grammar, and you'll get a smile. So children aren't parrots. They're more like little scientists, testing guesses about a system no one has explained to them.

questions.q: What is the main point of the talk?
options: Parents should correct children's grammar more often.
Children work out grammar rules for themselves.
Children learn nouns earlier than they learn verbs.
Language experiments on young children are unreliable.
questions.why: 'The child can't be copying. What she's done is work out a rule'; 'children aren't parrots'.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention the word "goed"?
options: To show that children hear adults make mistakes
To explain why the past tense is taught at school
To give evidence that children are not simply imitating
To illustrate a word that children find hard to pronounce
questions.why: 'No adult says goed. The child can't be copying.'

questions.q: What did the experiment with the imaginary creature show?
options: Children can make plurals of unfamiliar words.
Children remember drawings better than words.
Children enjoy invented words more than real ones.
Children learn plurals by repeating their parents.
questions.why: The children said 'wugs' although 'they'd never heard that word in their lives, so they couldn't have memorized its plural'.

questions.q: What does the professor imply about parents' corrections?
options: They are the main way children learn grammar.
They usually leave young children confused.
They happen more often with older children.
They are too rarely about grammar to teach it.
questions.why: Corrections tend 'to be about facts, not grammar', so they cannot be the source of children's grammar.

email.scenario: You are taking a marketing course, and your group of four is scheduled to give its final presentation next Monday. One member of your group, who prepared the section on survey results, has just learned that she will be away at a national swimming competition that day. The rest of the group does not want to present without her. You decide to write to your instructor, Professor Lindqvist.
email.subject: Group 3 presentation on Monday
bullets: Describe the problem your group has with the presentation date.
Suggest one or two possible solutions.
Ask how the change might affect your group's grade.
email.model:
Dear Professor Lindqvist,

I am writing on behalf of Group 3 in your marketing class. We are scheduled to give our final presentation next Monday, but one of our members, Aiko Tanaka, has been selected for a national swimming competition and will be out of town that day. Aiko prepared the section on our survey results, so it would be difficult for the rest of us to present it well without her.

We would like to suggest two possible solutions. We could exchange dates with one of the groups presenting on Wednesday, if one of them agrees. Alternatively, Aiko could record her part in advance, and we would play the video during our presentation on Monday.

Could you please tell us which of these you would accept? We would also like to ask whether presenting on a different day, or with a recorded section, would affect our grade.

Thank you for your understanding.

Sincerely,
Rahul Mehta

professor.name: Dr. Moreau
professor.post: This week, we are examining how universities design their degree programs. At many universities, students must complete general education courses in fields unrelated to their major, so an engineering student may have to study literature and a history student may have to take a science class. Some educators see this as essential to a complete education, whereas others consider it a waste of students' time and money. What is your view? Should universities require every student to take courses outside their major? Why or why not?

students.name: Lucas
students.post: I support the requirement. Most of us chose our majors at eighteen, before we had tried many subjects. A required course in another field can reveal an interest we never knew we had. My cousin started in accounting, took a required geology class, and ended up changing her major. Without that rule, she would never have found the career she loves.

students.name: Yuna
students.post: I see it differently. University is already expensive, and every required course outside my major costs money and delays the classes I actually need for my career. If I want to learn about art or history, I can read books or watch free lectures online. Universities should let adults decide how to spend their own time and tuition.

discussion.model: In my view, universities should keep a requirement for courses outside the major, but it should be small and flexible. I understand Yuna's concern about cost; nobody wants to pay for classes that feel irrelevant. However, I think she overlooks how much working life changes. Many graduates end up in jobs that did not exist when they started their degrees, and they need skills from several fields to adapt. A programmer who has studied psychology, for example, can design software that people actually enjoy using. Lucas mentions discovering new interests, and I would add that mixed classes also teach students to work with people who think differently from them. To limit the cost, universities could require only three or four such courses and let students choose freely among them. That way, the requirement broadens students' education without holding them back.

interview.scenario: You have agreed to take part in a research study about sleep habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

questions.q: Thank you for joining me today. To start, I'd like to hear about a typical night. What time do you usually go to bed and get up, and what do you do in the last hour before you sleep?
questions.model: On a normal weekday, I go to bed at around half past eleven and get up at seven, so I sleep for about seven and a half hours. In the last hour before bed, I try to follow the same routine. First, I prepare my bag and my clothes for the next morning so that I don't have to rush. Then I take a warm shower and read a few pages of a novel. I have to admit that I often look at my phone as well, even though I know it keeps me awake longer. On weekends, I go to bed much later and sleep until nine or ten.

questions.q: Some people do their best work early in the morning, while others feel more awake late at night. Which kind of person are you, and how does that affect the way you plan your day?
questions.model: I am definitely a morning person. My mind is clearest between about seven and eleven, so I plan my day around those hours. I do the tasks that need the most concentration, such as writing essays or solving math problems, before lunch. In the afternoon, I feel slower, so I use that time for easier things like answering messages, shopping, or going to the gym. By ten at night, I can hardly keep my eyes open, and anything I study then, I forget by the next day. My friends who are night owls think this is strange, but getting up early suits me.

questions.q: Now I'd like to hear your opinion. Some people say that students today do not get enough sleep because of smartphones and social media. Do you agree? Why or why not?
questions.model: I mostly agree. Many students I know take their phones to bed and plan to check one message, but then they keep watching videos for an hour. The content never ends, so it is hard to stop. Messages also arrive late at night, and people feel they must reply at once. However, I don't think phones are the only cause. Students also lose sleep because of homework, part-time jobs, and early classes. Even without a phone, a student who finishes work at eleven and has a class at eight will be tired. So phones make the problem worse, but they did not create it.

questions.q: Here is my last question. Some schools have moved the start of the school day to a later hour so that teenagers can sleep longer. Do you think more schools should do this? Why or why not?
questions.model: Yes, I think more schools should start later, at least for teenagers. When I was in high school, my first class began at half past seven, and most of us were half asleep. We did not learn much in that first hour, so the time was wasted. If classes began an hour later, students would be more awake, and I believe their grades and their mood would improve. Of course, there are practical problems. Parents who start work early may have difficulty taking their children to school, and sports practice would finish later in the evening. Still, I think these problems can be solved, and well-rested students are worth the effort.
